🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.25% (intraday, 7-year +18bp). At trading day 16 (last close) it was -1.11% against a five-campaign average of -1.01% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.28%. The 10-year is +22bp since the hike vs a +13bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 719bp against a five-year average of 410bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +38bp and BB +35bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.21 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+2bp).
  • Stocks: US and European stocks closed higher Friday. Japan was flat and fear stayed low.
  • FX: The dollar edged up and the euro sits below its average levels. Some yen and real data look inconsistent.
  • Technicals: US stocks are unusually stretched above their averages. Historically this often stalls before trends turn.
  • Sectors: This week money went to defensive sectors. Tech still leads over the month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Most corporate debt still looks calm. The riskiest junk bonds are under the most strain since 2020.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate. The main risks are an oil and war shock and the weakest borrowers.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is cooling slowly. A large share of prices is still rising fast.
  • Tech Bubble: Prices are well below the 2000 mania, but credit, volatility and financial conditions look as complacent as they did then.
  • Earnings & IPOs: JPMorgan opens bank earnings Tuesday. Delta had the biggest expected price swing. The US IPO calendar is thin.
  • Iran: The war resumed after the ceasefire lapsed, while talks continue through intermediaries.
  • Warsh: The Fed is likely to pause soon, with more hikes possible if inflation runs hot.
  • Week Ahead: Inflation data, retail sales, big-bank earnings and a Warsh speech.

PM, Fri Oct 09 close. Risk assets rose a second day. The S&P 500 gained 46.18 points to 7811.54 (+0.59%), the Nasdaq Composite rose 172.83 to 27366.17 (+0.64%) and the Dow led, up 423.31 to 51654.95 (+0.83%). The Russell 2000 added 0.46%. The VIX fell 0.57 to 14.84. Europe did better than the US: the STOXX 600 rose 0.97%, the FTSE 100 1.06% and the Euro Stoxx 50 0.76%. The Nikkei was flat (-0.02%). Long-dated sovereign yields fell outside the US: the JGB 10Y dropped 7.5bp to 3.018%, the Gilt 10Y 3.8bp to 5.443% and the Bund 10Y 1.4bp to 3.481%. The US curve flattened: the 2Y rose 2.92bp to 4.7869%, the 10Y rose 1.1bp to 5.2378% and the 30Y slipped 0.45bp to 5.5956%. Metals rallied: gold +1.49%, silver +2.79%, copper +1.88%. Brent held above $100 at 104.41. The biggest story is under the surface, in high-yield credit. Headline HY OAS is only 3.10%, but the computed Bloomberg Caa–B gap is 719bp. That is the 100th percentile of the past five years, well above its 5-year average of about 410bp, and the widest since 2020-04-24. It widened 41bp in a week, 97bp in a month and 204bp in three months. Caa OAS alone is 1014bp, up 226bp over three months. The FRED ICE BofA cross-check agrees: the CCC–B gap is 937bp, the 100th percentile on its full history. Is the rot spreading up the ladder? Over the past month, partly yes. Single-B widened 38bp to 295bp and Ba widened 35bp to 189bp. The HY–IG gap widened 37bp. This week, however, both B (-15bp) and Ba (-6bp) tightened while Caa kept widening. That looks like stress concentrating in the weakest names rather than spreading this week. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen to 0.52 from 0.28 a month ago, so the CCC and B moves are becoming more connected. It is still below its 5-year median of 0.70. IG is barely touched: 81bp, +2bp over the month, 29th percentile over five years. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Compared with the prior session, sentiment is complacent at the index level (stocks at 100th-percentile stretch, VIX under 15) and fragile in the credit tail. The backdrop adds to that: Iran escalation, Brent above $100, a Fed that hiked in September, and CPI plus the big-bank earnings kickoff next week.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.44 vol points (3th percentile of the 38 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 98.5 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 108bp (steeper by 31bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (92bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 8 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 57/100 — Sticky but slowly cooling. The underlying trend measures are all labeled 'falling' and sit around their historical middle (computed Core-Trend Sub-Score, rendered separately). Core PCE YoY at 3.00759 is stuck around 3%. Breadth is the problem: per the Dallas Fed distribution, 28.9% of the PCE basket is rising faster than 5% (13.2% above 10% plus 15.7% at 5–10%), and only 25.8% is falling. With flexible CPI at 4.9424 and oil above $90, headline risk tilts up even as core trends ease. That is enough to keep a hawkish Fed engaged but not enough to demand aggressive further hikes.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (44x) ≈ 25% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The setup resembles roughly 1997–98 more than early 2000. Valuations are high but not manic outside semis. The conditions that let a mania build (cheap credit, low volatility, loose financial conditions, capital crowded into US equities) are in place, while the classic trigger, a rolling-over economy with an inverted curve, is missing. The CCC blowout is the one crack: in 2000 the tail of credit also cracked before equities did. The analyst-estimate inputs (top-10 concentration ~40%, CAPE ~39x, market cap/GDP ~215%, IPO froth ~45/100, LT EPS growth expectations ~65/100) were NOT web-verified in this run because the search budget went to the mandated news topics. Treat them as rough judgment, not data. IPO froth is tempered: the near-term US calendar looks thin, and the mega-listings (SpaceX/OpenAI/Anthropic) remain anticipated rather than priced.

⚔️Iran War

The conflict has resumed. One tracker lists the status as 'war resumed' as of Oct 8, after the June ceasefire memorandum expired unextended on Aug 17 (iranwarlive.com). - Diplomacy: Iranian FM Araghchi said talks with the US continue through intermediaries, and Tehran is reviewing Washington's response to its 'seven-day plan'. President Pezeshkian said Iran revised its peace-talk proposals (CBS live updates). - US posture: Trump has said the US will not resume strikes before the Nov 3 midterms. Separately, The Atlantic reported (via CBS) that the White House asked the Pentagon to prepare strike options before the midterms. The sources do not reconcile these. - Sanctions: Treasury targeted 17 vessels and said the action 'effectively neutralizes the vast majority of Iran's remaining shadow fleet network'. - Regional: Iran-backed Houthis struck Riyadh's main airport, killing three Saudi citizens, and several airlines suspended Riyadh flights (CBS). Market read (analyst): Brent at 104.41 already prices a meaningful risk premium. Gulf strikes and shadow-fleet sanctions keep upside tail risk alive, and a credible diplomatic track is the main downside risk for oil. These are live-blog snapshots with mixed timestamps, so verify before acting.

Sources: CBS News live updates: Houthis kill 3 in strike on Saudi airport as Trump rules out pre-midterms strikes · CBS News: Trump promises not to resume strikes before midterm elections · Iran War Live Map tracker · NBC News: Iran War coverage

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the next FOMC (inferred). Warsh's Fed hiked 25bp on Sept 16 to 3.75–4.00%, the first hike since 2023. The September dots showed one more hike in 2026 as the median. Calendar commentary since then says officials (Jefferson, Williams, Waller, Bowman) have alluded to an October pause, and that implied October hike odds fell to about 20% after weak jobs data (NFP 29.0 in our feed). A hot CPI on Oct 14 is the main path back to a hike.

~1 YEAR

Inferred: 1–2 more hikes over the next year if oil-driven headline inflation and core PCE around 3% persist. Warsh said inflation has been 'too high for too long' and that he wants a 'timelier return' to 2%. He also favours a 'quieter' Fed and says he is 'not in the forward guidance business', so expect fewer signals and more data-dependent surprises. A pivot to cuts within a year would likely need CCC-type credit stress to broaden or labor to weaken sharply. That is analyst inference from his record, not a stated plan.

Warsh's on-record pattern since June: a hawkish inflation focus (Jackson Hole Aug 28 flagged that hikes may be needed in the coming months), a refusal to commit to forward guidance, and the Strait of Hormuz cited as the key pressure point keeping oil above $100. He speaks late Thursday Oct 15 (listed 11:30 PM ET by one calendar; verify the time). Expect him to reaffirm data dependence after CPI and retail sales. The 2Y rising 2.92bp today, more than the 10Y, shows the market leaning his way. Flag: the near-term and one-year calls are my inferences, not Fed statements.
